result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.add_gnp_graph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Add an Erdős-Rényi G(n,p) random graph to the current graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L5101-L5218){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.add_gnp_graph( n, p, directed=None, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![G(n, p) random graph](/assets/graphs/add-gnp-graph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Three random graphs on the same ring of eight nodes for edge probability p=0.1, 0.3, and 0.5. Each possible edge appears independently, so the drawings gain edges as p grows (3, 8, and 14 here) with no pattern to which pairs are joined." width="100%"} Each possible edge is included independently with probability `p`. This model is useful for generating random graphs with a specific edge density. The method adds `n` new, unlabelled nodes and then flips a biased coin for every possible edge among them. In an undirected graph each of the `n(n - 1) / 2` unordered pairs is considered once; in a directed graph each of the `n(n - 1)` ordered pairs is considered, so `u -> v` and `v -> u` are drawn independently. Self-loops are never created. The number of edges is therefore random, with an expected value of `p` times the number of pairs, and the graph's density will be close to `p`. Existing nodes are left untouched and never connected to the new ones. G(n, p) graphs are the classic baseline random network, used for: - null models: checking whether a real network's clustering, path lengths, or motifs differ from what random wiring at the same density would give - generating test graphs of a chosen density for benchmarking algorithms - exploring threshold behavior, e.g. the graph becomes connected with high probability once `p` exceeds about `ln(n) / n` Every pair is examined, so the running time grows as `n^2` even for very small `p=`; for large sparse graphs with a known edge count, `add_gnm_graph()` is the closely related alternative. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes to add. The new nodes have no labels and get the next available node IDs. [p]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Probability that any given pair of the new nodes is joined, in the range `[0.0, 1.0]`. `p=0.0` gives `n` isolated nodes, and `p=1.0` gives a complete graph. Values outside the range raise a `ValueError`. [directed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[bool]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Leave as `None` (default) to generate edges according to the graph's own directedness. Passing the graph's own setting (`graph.is_directed()`) does the same thing. Passing a value that differs from it is intended to generate the edges as if the graph had that directedness, but this path is currently broken and raises an `AttributeError`; create the `Graph` with the directedness you want instead. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same `n=` and `p=` always gives the same edges. If `None` (default), the result differs on every call. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `p=` is outside `[0.0, 1.0]`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Each of the `n(n-1)/2` possible edges is included independently with probability `p`, so the expected edge count is `n(n-1)/2 * p` -- for `n=50` and `p=0.1` that's `122.5` edges on average, and the exact count varies with the random seed. The density lands close to `p`: ::: {#0e278c8a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_gnp_graph(n=50, p=0.1, seed=23) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges(), round(graph.get_density(), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (50, 109, 0.089) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph both orientations of every pair are drawn separately, so there are twice as many candidate edges and roughly twice as many edges result: ::: {#afb9c22e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} directed = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_gnp_graph(n=50, p=0.1, seed=23) directed.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 230 ``` ::: ::: The connectivity threshold for `n=100` is about `ln(100) / 100`, or roughly `0.046`. Below it the random graph typically falls apart into pieces, while above it the graph is usually connected: ::: {#b8710f0a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ (p, ec.Graph().add_gnp_graph(n=100, p=p, seed=23).is_connected()) for p in (0.02, 0.05, 0.1) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [(0.02, False), (0.05, True), (0.1, True)] ``` ::: :::
